own_scenes.desc: Yvette Marie Stevens, presidenta del sindicato de estudiantes negros y del Afro-Arts Theater de Chicago, tomó el nombre de Chaka en un desayuno de los Panteras. Se unió en 1970 a Rufus, una banda multirracial de Chicago (Andre Fischer, Tony Maiden, Bobby Watson, Kevin Murphy). En Los Ángeles, Stevie Wonder les dio «Tell Me Something Good», hecha para la sensualidad de Chaka (Grammy 1974), y Ray Parker Jr. «You Got the Love»: cinco discos de oro seguidos (Rags to Rufus, Rufusized, Rufus Featuring Chaka Khan, Ask Rufus, Street Player). Chaka coescribía y arreglaba («I’m a Woman (I’m a Backbone)»), un modelo de feminidad negra rotunda; en solitario se pasó al disco. Lo que el soul llama cantante, el funk lo convierte en una banda entera.

refs.q: With everyone getting into the picture in the mid-seventies, a female-led funk band was inevitable.
refs.para: With everyone getting into the picture in the mid-seventies, a female-led funk band was inevitable. One such act was Rufus, led by the sassy and stunning singer Chaka Khan. Rich robust black femininity never had a better role model than the youthful Chaka. Born Yvette Marie Stevens, she was a high school whiz, performing in student politics (Black Student Union president) and in the local Afro-Arts Theater (where Fred and Maurice White—later of Earth, Wind & Fire—used to hand out and soak up the African spirituality/free jazz/vegetarian/kalimba vibe). She took the name Chaka while working at a Black Panther Party breakfast program in Chicago. Although she isn’t known to speak specifically of racial issues, Chaka nevertheless brings her roots to the forefront.
refs.chapter: Cap. 14: United Funk: The Shining Star

refs.q: More symbolically than literally, Chaka Khan provided a leadership role and a strong female image with the band
refs.para: More symbolically than literally, Chaka Khan provided a leadership role and a strong female image with the band, arranging songs and cowriting such monster hits as “Sweet Thing,” “You Got the Love,” and “Stay.” Her strong identity was also revealed in the crunching rendition of “I’m a Woman (and I’m a Backbone)” from the group’s Rufusized LP.
